name: Timestamp
description: How an instant is stored, transported and compared. Time is the classic place for two implementations to disagree quietly, so every rule here is normative for both.
principle: The database and the wire carry UTC only. A local time exists in exactly one place: the browser, at the moment of rendering. Nothing behind the frontend ever knows the user's zone.

storage.sqlite: INTEGER, milliseconds since the Unix epoch
rules: PostgreSQL columns are timestamptz, never timestamp. A bare timestamp discards the zone on write and the two implementations then disagree about what they read back.
SQLite has no time type. The integer is milliseconds since 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z, signed, so instants before 1970 remain representable.
The session and the database connection run in UTC. Neither implementation may depend on the server's local zone, and neither may set a per-connection time zone.
A timestamp on the wire is a decimal string of milliseconds since the Unix epoch, like every other number in these contracts. Not ISO-8601, not a locale format, never an offset.
The API neither sends nor accepts a local time. A request carrying an offset is a client error, not something to convert.
NULL is JSON null. It is never 0 — 0 is a valid instant (1970-01-01T00:00:00Z), and an implementation that conflates the two produces records that claim to be older than Gradido.
Logs may render ISO-8601 with a trailing Z for humans. That is presentation, not the contract.
wire.rationale: C has no date type. Milliseconds parse and format identically in both languages with no calendar code, and they compare and sort as integers. ISO-8601 would need a parser in C whose edge cases (fractional digits, offsets, leap seconds) are exactly where two implementations drift apart.

rules: Higher precision is truncated toward the past (floor), never rounded. Rounding up can place a created_at in the future, and a record that does not exist yet fails validation elsewhere.
Floor applies to negative values as well, so truncation stays monotonic across the epoch.

One request takes its 'now' once and reuses it. Rows written by the same interaction must carry the same created_at — a per-statement CURRENT_TIMESTAMP drifts between statements and makes a transaction's rows disagree about when it happened.
'now' is the UTC system clock. Neither implementation may derive it from a database function, so that both produce the same value under test.
The frontend renders in the browser's zone and locale, from the millisecond value it received.
This is deliberately not contracted further: rendering concerns one implementation, and a disagreement about a date format is not a backend bug. See AGENTS.md, working rule 3.

open.question: In which zone does a calendar-based contribution cycle begin?
open.detail: ContributionCycleType has DAILY implemented and MONTH, QUARTER, YEAR planned. A rolling window needs no zone — ALIAS_QUOTA_WINDOW_MS is simply a duration. A calendar boundary does: 'daily' has to start somewhere, and midnight UTC, midnight in the community's zone and midnight for the member are three different instants that pay out on different days.
open.why_it_matters: This is the one place where UTC-everywhere is not automatically the answer, and where both implementations would otherwise each guess. It decides amounts, not display.
open.status: unanswered — check what legacy does before the first cycle-based contribution is rebuilt
